If the firing pulses are suddenly removed, the steady state voltage (\(v_0\)) waveform of the converter will become
questions.explanation:
Single phase half controlled converter.
As load is highly inductive, it means laod current is continuous and almost constant.

\[\begin{aligned} &\text{During,}\\ &0 \lt \omega t \lt \alpha \\ &\text{freewheeling by }T_2D_1, V_0=0\\ &\alpha \lt \omega t \lt \pi \\ &T_1D_1 \text{ conducts }V_0=V_s\\ &\pi \lt \omega t \lt \pi+\alpha \\ &\text{freewheeling by }T_1D_2, V_0=0\\ &\pi+\alpha \lt \omega t \lt 2\pi \\ &T_2D_2 \text{ conducts }V_0=-V_s\\ &T_1 \text{ is again triggered at }2 \pi+\alpha \end{aligned}\]
So, during \(2\pi+\alpha \lt \omega t \lt 3\pi , T_1D_1\) conducts.
Now, if firing pulses are removed after \(T_1\) is triggered at \(2 \pi+\alpha\).
At \(\omega t=3 \pi+\alpha\), no firing pulse will be available to trigger \(T_2\). So, load current will flow through \(T_1D_2\) as load current is continuos. So during \(3 \pi+\alpha \lt \omega t \lt 4 \pi,\;\; T_1D_2\) will continue to conduct and \(V_0=0\).
At \(\omega t=4 \pi,\; D_1\) will become forward biassed and \(D_2\) will become reverse biased. So, \(D_1\) will conduct and \(T_1\) is already conducting.
So, load current will flow through \(T_1D_1\) and \(V_0=V_s\).

A 3-phase, 440 V, 50 Hz, 4-pole slip ring induction motor is feed from the rotor side through an auto-transformer and the stator is connected to a variable resistance as shown in the figure.

The motor is coupled to a 220 V, separately excited d.c generator feeding power to fixed resistance of 10 \(\Omega\). Two-wattmeter method is used to measure the input power to induction motor. The variable resistance is adjusted such the motor runs at 1410 rpm and the following readings were recorded

\(W_1=1800 W , W_2=-200 W\).

options: 90 rpm in the direction of rotation
90 rpm in the opposite direction of rotation
1500 rpm in the direction of rotation
1500 rpm in the opposite direction of rotation
questions.explanation:
If the three phase supply is given to the rotor winding through an autotransformer, the three phase rotor current will generate a rotating field in the air-gap, rotating at the synchronous speed woth respect to rotor. If the rotor is kept stationary, this rotating field will also rotate in the gap at the synchronous speed voltage and current will be induced in the stator winding and a torque will be developed. If rotor is allowed to move, it will rotate as per the Lenz's law, opposing the rotation of the rotating field decreasing the induced voltage in the stator winding. Thus at a particular speed, the frequency of the stator circuit will correspond to the slip speed.
Synchronous speed,
\(N_s=\frac{120f}{P}=\frac{120 \times 50}{4}=1500 \; \text{rpm}\)
Rotor speed,
\(N_r=1410 \; \text{rpm}\)
\(\text{Slip}=\frac{N_s-N_r}{N_s}\)
\(\;\;=\frac{1500-1410}{1500}=0.06\)
Slip frequency induced in stator
\(sf=0.06 \times 50=3 Hz\)
Slip speed \(= \frac{120 \times 3}{4}=90\; \text{rpm}\)
As stator magnetic field rotates 90 rpm in the opposite direction of the rotation of rotor, therefore, speed of the stator field with respect to rotor \(=1410+90=1500 rpm\)
